name: Turlington's Balsam

lead:
Turlington's Balsam was a patent remedy created by the English merchant Robert Turlington. It received a royal patent in 1744, listing 27 ingredients.
Its patent application named kidney and bladder stones, colic and inward weakness, and a later brochure expanded the list of uses. It is documented here as history rather than as a skin treatment.

paras: It was sold in distinctively shaped bottles; Turlington changed the bottle design several times and introduced an embossed tablet-shaped bottle in 1754, because patents covered the medicine and not its packaging.
No clinical data exist. The ingredients and modern availability are not documented.

chain: Balsam sold as a general remedy
angle.text: It was marketed as a general remedy. No source reviewed documents a specific appearance use.

lead: Turlington's Balsam was a patent medicine created by Robert Turlington, an English merchant, who obtained a royal patent from George II in 1744 [1]. It became popular in England and the American colonies [1].

Its application listed 27 ingredients and claimed it treated kidney and bladder stones, colic and inward weakness; a later 46-page brochure expanded the claims [1]. Appearance-related use is not documented.

paras: The patent is considered one of the earliest medicinal patents; the earliest was granted in 1698 for Epsom salts [1].
Within about ten years of the patent, Turlington changed the bottle shape at least four times, using packaging to distinguish the product from copies [1].

timeline.event: Royal patent granted by George II [1]
